## Simulated data
Every output on this page comes from the package's simulated data. It shows what this step produces and how to read it. It says nothing about any real state: every gap, ratio and rate here comes from how the data were generated.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(stateELP)
```

## What this step answers

Suppose the exit threshold were set only by how English language
proficiency (ELP) lines up with proficiency on the content test. Where would
it land, and how does the current rule compare?

The stage works on the ELP **level**. A **cut** is a candidate threshold on
that level. At each cut, every current English learner (EL) is classified
twice: *ready to exit* or not by ELP level (at or above the cut), and
*proficient* or not on the same year's content test. Two statistics
summarize how the classifications line up:

- **Decision consistency** (agreement): the share of students the two
  classifications agree on.
- **Youden's J**: sensitivity plus specificity, minus one. **Sensitivity**
  is the share of proficient students the cut calls ready; **specificity**
  is the share of not-proficient students it calls not ready. J is 0 when
  a cut separates nothing and 1 when it separates perfectly.

**J is the primary statistic**, and the cut where it is highest is the **J
optimum**. The reason is the **base rate**, the share of current ELs who are
proficient. It is usually well below one half, and then agreement is pulled
toward calling everyone "not ready". J weights the two kinds of error equally
*as rates*, however common each group is.

**Why the level, not the scale score.** The exit rule is written on the
level, so the rule and the J optimum can share one axis. The spec declares a
range only for the level scale; it has no map from scale scores to levels
(`elp$cuts` is `NULL`). Scale scores depend on grade, so a scale-score
optimum would not compare across grades. And some instruments report only a
level.

[Check 3](check3.html) shows content scores by ELP band. Check 4 turns the
same pairing into a yes/no classification. The two are read together.

## Sample

**Cross-sectional: every current EL in one grade and one year with both a
same-year annual ELP level and a same-year content score in one subject.**
The level is on the component the spec names for every stage
(`spec$elp$headline`): the "Overall Composite" in the simulated spec, which
is also what the exit rule is written on.

This is the current-EL part of Check 3's paired cross-section, **not** the
entry cohort of Checks 1 and 2 (students who entered EL status in the same
grade and year, followed forward). Left out are former ELs and English-only
students (they have no ELP level to classify), students on an alternate
academic assessment (another score scale), current ELs with no annual ELP
level that year, and any level outside the spec's declared scale (counted in
`res$meta$n_out_of_scale`).

Each grade × subject × year is its own **panel**; grades are never pooled.
By default `run_check4()` takes the panel Check 3's `compute_panel()`
derives: the spec's first academic subject, its first tested grade, and the
latest year with academic rows. Both stages call the same function, so they
describe the same students. Scores are paired within the school year, not to
the day.

## Status in the package

::: {.callout-note}
## First pass built
The stage computes and renders one grade × subject panel. Three of its six
result slots are built; the other three are `NULL` by design.
:::

| Slot | Status | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `$consistency_curve` | Built | Classification counts and agreement at every candidate cut |
| `$youden_j` | Built | The same rows, plus sensitivity, specificity and J |
| `$j_optimal` | Built | One row per panel: J optimum, highest agreement, current rule, error-tolerance reading |
| `$candidate_region` | `NULL`: later pass | The region across grades, annotated with Check 1's reliability |
| `$dependence` | `NULL`: no package support | The copula / Kendall's-tau dependence analysis |
| `$policy_as_whole` | `NULL`: Type-gated, not built | The whole multi-criterion rule as a classifier (Types 2–6) |

What this means for you:

- **One panel per call.** Use the `subject`, `grade` and `year` arguments
  for others; "How to read it" loops over grades.
- **The candidate region is yours to write for now**, by hand.
- **Prep 3 is not built**, so the error-tolerance answer is read straight
  from `spec$policy$error_tolerance`. The simulated spec says `"unknown"`.
- **Some choices await confirmation** in the package's build notes: the
  suppression rule, tie-breaking (lowest tied cut wins), the per-student
  reading of error tolerance, and the comparison with Check 3.

## Before you start

You need:

- **An `el_data` bundle with an academic table** (see [Setup](setup.html)).
- **Decimal ELP levels** if your instrument reports them. The candidate cuts
  are the distinct levels the delivery carries, so whole numbers give few.
- **A spec that declares** the level scale and bands (`elp$level_scale`,
  `elp$bands`); the exit rule as structured terms (`policy$exit`); the
  academic subjects, grades and cut scores (`academic`) with the proficient
  level (`policy$academic_benchmark$proficient_level`); the suppression
  minimum (`policy$suppression$min_cell`), the smallest group a published
  number may describe; and Prep 3's answer (`policy$error_tolerance`), or
  `"unknown"`.
- **Check 3's results at hand.** Check 4 does not need them to run, but you
  read the two together.

Build the spec and bundle once, and look at what the stage will read:

```{r}
spec <- read_el_spec("00_SIM_EL_Spec")
bundle <- as_el_data(el_long_sim, roster = el_roster_sim,
                     academic = academic_long_sim, spec = spec)

spec_headline_label(spec)              # the ELP component the stages use
spec$elp$level_scale$range             # the level scale the cuts live on
spec$policy$exit$pathways[[1]]$rule    # the current rule, as written
spec$policy$error_tolerance$costlier_error
spec_min_cell(spec)
```

Then check which panel the stage will draw, and how many students it can
draw on:

```{r}
panel <- compute_panel(bundle, spec)
panel[c("subject", "grade", "year")]

cov <- el_coverage(bundle)
cov[cov$YEAR == panel$year & cov$GRADE == panel$grade,
    c("YEAR", "GRADE", "N_CURRENT", "N_CURRENT_ELP", "N_ALTERNATE")]
```

`N_ALTERNATE` counts current ELs on the alternate ELP form. They have no
annual level, so they are outside the sample too. The paired sample is
smaller than `N_CURRENT_ELP`, because each student also needs a content score
in the subject.

**What degrades to `NULL`.** The stage never crashes on a missing input; it
empties the slot and says why in `res$meta$note`. With no academic table, or
a spec that declares no academic subject (the shipped ELPA21 example points
to a separate academic spec), every slot is `NULL`. So is a panel that
cannot be derived; the R error is kept in `res$meta$panel_error`. With no
proficiency cut, or no student with both scores, the curves are `NULL`. If
the exit rule has no term on the component's own level, the curves are
drawn without a rule marked, and `res$meta$threshold_note` says why.

## Run it

```{r}
res <- run_check4(bundle, spec)
names(res)
```

`run_check4()` takes the panel and calls three functions in order. You can
run them yourself to inspect each step:

```{r}
curve <- compute_consistency_curve(bundle, spec, panel)
yj    <- compute_youden_j(curve)
opt   <- compute_j_optimal(yj, spec)
identical(opt, res$j_optimal)
```

For another panel: `run_check4(bundle, spec, subject = "Math", grade = "8")`.
A subject or grade the spec does not declare is an error, not a silent
switch.

```{r}
#| include: false
o <- res$j_optimal
y <- res$youden_j
shown <- y[!y$SUPPRESSED, ]
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
num <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
big <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
k <- match(o$J_CUT, shown$CUT)
nb <- shown[max(1, k - 2):min(nrow(shown), k + 1), ]
nb_txt <- paste0(nb$CUT_LABEL, " (J = ", num(nb$J), ")", collapse = ", ")
notes <- c("axis_note", "pairing_note", "threshold_note", "resolution_note",
           "dependence_note", "policy_as_whole_note")
na_notes <- notes[vapply(notes, function(x) is.na(res$meta[[x]]), logical(1))]
na_notes_txt <- if (length(na_notes)) {
  paste0("the ", paste(sub("_note$", "", na_notes), collapse = " and "),
         if (length(na_notes) > 1) " notes" else " note")
} else "none of them"
side_txt <- switch(if (is.na(o$THRESHOLD_SIDE)) "none" else o$THRESHOLD_SIDE,
  above  = "sits above the J optimum",
  below  = "sits below the J optimum",
  same   = "classifies exactly as the J optimum",
  within = "falls inside the suppressed range around the J optimum",
  "cannot be placed against an optimum")
agree_where <- paste0(o$AGREE_CUT_LABEL,
  if (isTRUE(o$AGREE_CUT == max(shown$CUT))) " (the highest cut that can be shown)" else "")
agree_vs_floor <- if (o$AGREE <= o$AGREE_FLOOR) {
  "does not even beat that floor"
} else {
  paste0("beats that floor by ", round(100 * (o$AGREE - o$AGREE_FLOOR)),
         " percentage points")
}
```

## What you get

### The Sample statement

Read it first:

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(res$meta$sample)
```

### The figure

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.5
plot_consistency_curve(res$youden_j, res$j_optimal, spec)
```

Agreement is on top and J below, each on its own vertical scale. The dashed
line is the J optimum, the dotted line the current rule, and the circle
agreement's highest reportable point. Suppressed cuts are not drawn.

### The optimum

The stage report's summary table:

```{r}
ft_check4_optimum(res)
```

The full `$j_optimal` row carries more:

```{r}
o <- res$j_optimal
o[, c("N", "BASE_RATE", "J_CUT", "J", "N_J_TIED", "J_MAX_HIDDEN")]
o[, c("AGREE_CUT", "AGREE", "AGREE_FLOOR", "OPTIMA_DIVERGE")]
o[, c("THRESHOLD", "THRESHOLD_CUT", "THRESHOLD_SIDE", "J_AT_THRESHOLD")]
o[, c("IMPLIED_COST_RATIO", "COSTLIER_ERROR", "LEAN", "NO_OPTIMUM")]
```

- `BASE_RATE`: the share of the panel's current ELs who are proficient.
- `J_CUT`, `J`: the J optimum and its value. `N_J_TIED` counts cuts tied at
  the maximum. `J_MAX_HIDDEN` is `TRUE` when a suppressed cut sits between
  the optimum and the shown cuts either side of it. The optimum is then
  located only to within the range from `J_SHOWN_BELOW` to `J_SHOWN_ABOVE`.
  `FALSE` does not promise that no suppressed cut farther away has a higher
  J.
- `AGREE_CUT`, `AGREE`: agreement's highest reportable point.
  `AGREE_FLOOR` is the agreement of calling *every* student not ready (one
  minus the base rate). `OPTIMA_DIVERGE` is `TRUE` when the two peak at
  different cuts.
- `THRESHOLD`: the current rule, read from the spec. `THRESHOLD_CUT` is the
  observed cut it classifies as (a 4.5 rule with nobody at exactly 4.5
  classifies like the next observed level). `THRESHOLD_SIDE` places that cut
  `"above"`, `"below"`, the `"same"` as, or `"within"` the hidden range
  around the J optimum.
- `IMPLIED_COST_RATIO`, `COSTLIER_ERROR`, `LEAN`: the error-tolerance
  reading, explained below.
- `NO_OPTIMUM`: `NA` when an optimum is reported; otherwise
  `"suppressed"`, `"no_variation"` (nobody or everybody proficient) or
  `"uninformative"` (no cut has J above zero, and none was hidden).

### The curve, cut by cut

`$youden_j` has one row per candidate cut. The cuts that can be shown:

```{r}
y <- res$youden_j
y[!y$SUPPRESSED,
  c("CUT", "TP", "FP", "FN", "TN", "AGREE", "SENSITIVITY", "SPECIFICITY", "J")]
```

The four counts are a two-by-two table at that cut. `TP`: proficient and at
or above the cut. `FP`: not proficient but at or above it (a premature exit,
if this were the rule). `FN`: proficient but below it (held back). `TN`: not
proficient and below it. `AGREE` is `(TP + TN) / N`; `J` is
`TP / (TP + FN) + TN / (TN + FP) - 1`. `ft_check4_curve(res)` is the
report's version, listing every cut with suppressed ones as dashes.

**Suppression.** Here `r sum(!y$SUPPRESSED)` of `r nrow(y)` cuts can be
shown. A blanked cut keeps its row, `CUT` and `N`; its counts and rates are
`NA` and `SUPPRESSED` is `TRUE`. A cut is blanked when one of its cells is a
non-zero count below `min_cell`, or when subtracting it from a neighboring
published count, including Check 3's band counts, would reveal a group that
small. And if the ELP bands whose shares Check 3 cannot show hold, together,
a small group of proficient or not-proficient students, every cut is
blanked. The J optimum is the best *reportable* cut. Small panels can lose
the curve entirely: in the package's own experiments, most panels of about
160 students reported no optimum.

### The notes

The sentences the report prints beside the figure:

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(check4_optimum_note(res), "\n\n")
cat(check4_tolerance_note(res), "\n")
```

`res$meta` also holds `axis_note`, `pairing_note`, `threshold_note`,
`resolution_note`, `dependence_note` and `policy_as_whole_note`. A note is
`NA` when it does not apply. Here that is true of `r na_notes_txt`.

### The empty slots

```{r}
vapply(res[c("candidate_region", "dependence", "policy_as_whole")],
       is.null, logical(1))
res$meta$pending
```

`$meta$pending` lists slots that apply to this spec but are not built.
`$dependence` is not listed: the method has no package support yet.

## How to read it

### The base-rate pull

Agreement equals the base rate times sensitivity plus (one minus the base
rate) times specificity. With a low base rate, specificity dominates:
calling everyone "not ready" already agrees for every non-proficient student.

In this panel `r pct(o$BASE_RATE)` of `r big(o$N)` current ELs are
proficient, so calling everyone not ready agrees `r pct(o$AGREE_FLOOR)` of
the time. Agreement's highest reportable point, `r pct(o$AGREE)` at
`r agree_where`, `r agree_vs_floor`.
J peaks at `r o$J_CUT_LABEL` (J = `r num(o$J)`). These come from the
generator's settings; they show the method's behavior, not a finding.

In general, when proficiency rises with level, agreement peaks where the
proficiency rate among students *at a level* crosses one half, and J where
it crosses the *overall base rate*. So when the base rate is below one half,
the J optimum sits at or below agreement's peak, usually well below.

**Confirm you are computing J, not agreement relabeled.** This is the
stage's checkpoint. The package tests it on a fixture with a 16% base rate
where the two optima differ by construction. On your own output:

```{r}
with(res$youden_j, all.equal(J, TP / (TP + FN) + TN / (TN + FP) - 1))
res$j_optimal$OPTIMA_DIVERGE
```

The first line recomputes J from the four counts. The second says whether
the two optima differ in this panel. `FALSE` is not by itself an error: the
two can land on the same cut, especially when the base rate is near one
half. What must hold is that the reported optimum is J's.

### The shape, not only the peak

A flat top means several cuts separate students almost equally well. Here
the shown cuts around the optimum read `r nb_txt`. The optimum alone
overstates how precisely the data locate a threshold, which is why the
stage's eventual output is a *region*.

### The current rule against the optimum

The current rule (level `r if (identical(o$THRESHOLD_OP, ">=")) "≥" else ">"`
`r o$THRESHOLD_LABEL`) `r side_txt` here, with J = `r num(o$J_AT_THRESHOLD)`
against `r num(o$J)` at the optimum. That difference is the separation the
rule gives up on this one criterion, content proficiency in this grade.

Read the right-hand end of the axis with care. A student still an EL at or
above the exit level is, in most states, in their final year, so those cuts
rest on students on their way out. In the simulated data every current EL at
or above 4.5 is in their exit year.

### Error tolerance: what J assumes

J weights the two errors equally **as rates**, not per student. Maximizing J
is the same as minimizing `FP + R × FN`, with
`R = (1 − base rate) / base rate`, reported as `IMPLIED_COST_RATIO`. Here
`R` is `r num(o$IMPLIED_COST_RATIO, 1)`: at the J optimum, holding back one
proficient student counts as much as exiting
`r num(o$IMPLIED_COST_RATIO, 1)` who are not proficient.

Prep 3 (not yet built) asks stakeholders which error is costlier for a
student: exiting them prematurely, or holding them longer than necessary.
The package reads the answer per student, and `LEAN` gives the side of the
reported J optimum it points to:

- **Premature exit costlier:** `"above"` whenever the base rate is at or
  below one half; otherwise `NA`.
- **Equal per student:** `"above"`, toward agreement's maximum, when the
  base rate is below one half, and `"below"` when it is above. It is
  `"at"` when the J optimum is itself agreement's maximum, beats the
  everyone-not-ready floor, and no suppressed cut lies above it.
- **Prolonged retention costlier:** `"below"` only if a hold is judged more
  than `R` times as costly. Prep 3 does not record how much, so `LEAN` is `NA`
  unless the base rate is at least one half (`R` at most 1).

Trying each answer on a copy of the spec (hypothetical answers, not anything
a state said):

```{r}
answers <- c("premature_exit", "equal", "prolonged_retention")
vapply(answers, function(a) {
  s <- spec
  s$policy$error_tolerance$costlier_error <- a
  compute_j_optimal(res$youden_j, s)$LEAN
}, character(1))
```

With `"unknown"`, `LEAN` is `NA` and the note says the question is open. A
stated asymmetry is a documented reason to land above or below the J
optimum: a values input, not a departure from the evidence. This
per-student reading awaits confirmation. To record a real answer, set
`costlier_error`, `asked_of`, `asked_date`, `rationale` and `source` under
`policy$error_tolerance` in your spec.

### Across grades

The report shows one panel, but the evidence is read across grades. Until
the candidate-region pass exists, run each grade and keep the panels apart:

```{r}
grades <- spec_academic_grades(spec, "ELA")
ela <- lapply(grades, function(g) {
  run_check4(bundle, spec, subject = "ELA", grade = g)
})
ela_opt <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(ela, function(r) r$j_optimal))
ela_opt[, c("GRADE", "N", "BASE_RATE", "J_CUT", "J", "J_MAX_HIDDEN",
            "AGREE_CUT", "THRESHOLD_SIDE")]
```

Each row is its own panel. Here the J optima run from
`r min(ela_opt$J_CUT)` to `r max(ela_opt$J_CUT)`, and the rule sits above
the optimum in `r sum(ela_opt$THRESHOLD_SIDE %in% "above")` of
`r nrow(ela_opt)` grades: patterns the simulation built in. Each panel takes
the latest year by default. On real data, look at whether the optima
cluster, which rows have `J_MAX_HIDDEN = TRUE`, and what Prep 2 found about
each grade's composition and Check 1 about attrition. Heavy attrition or a
large long-term EL share can move a grade's optimum for reasons unrelated to
the language threshold. This table is not the candidate region, and Check 1's
experimental `$grade_weights` are not used here.

### Beside Check 3

Treat convergence between Checks 3 and 4 as the strongest evidence. But
compare like with like. Check 3's `$landing` reports `LANDING_BAND` (the
first ELP band where half the students reach the cut) and `LANDING_CROSSING`
(the ELP *scale score*, a different axis, where a fitted logistic crosses
50%). Both mark where proficiency becomes more likely than not, which is
agreement's target, not J's. With a base rate below one half they should
land at or above the J optimum, or not appear at all. That gap is expected.
The informative comparisons are Check 3's band landing against Check 4's
agreement curve, and both against J.

## Pitfalls

- **Do not take the agreement peak as the optimal cut.** Use the J optimum,
  and run the checkpoint above.
- **Do not pool grades.** Each panel has its own base rate.
- **Do not report the J optimum as "the" threshold.** Report the shape, ties
  (`N_J_TIED`) and any hidden range (`J_MAX_HIDDEN`).
- **"Equal costs" means equal rates**, not equal per student.
- **Never lower `min_cell`** to recover suppressed cuts. Report that the
  panel is too small.
- **Whole-number levels against a fractional rule** (such as 4.5) trigger a
  `check4_coarse_levels` warning and a report callout. Ask for decimal
  levels.
- **Do not type the threshold.** It is read from `policy$exit`.
- **Do not place Check 3's logistic crossing on this axis.** It is a scale
  score; Check 4's cuts are levels.
- **Read the cuts at and above the exit level with care.** They rest on
  students in their final year as ELs.
- **This is a snapshot, not growth**: one grade, one year.
- **On simulated data the J optimum is machinery, not a finding.** It is set
  by the generator's parameters and by how the simulated exit rule thins the
  top of the scale.

## Decide before moving on

::: {.callout-tip}
## Decide before moving on
1. **A candidate region**, not necessarily a single number, supported by the
   balance of evidence across Checks 3 and 4. Note which grades and years
   carry the most and least reliable evidence, per Check 1.
2. **Record Prep 3's error-tolerance answer beside the region**, or that the
   question is still open, for the Decision stage.
:::

The package does not build the region yet, so write it down: the range of
cuts you consider supported, the grades that drive it, the grades you
discount and why, and where the current rule sits.

## Additional checks for multi-criterion exit rules

The spec declares the exit-criteria Types in `policy$exit$types` (Prep 1,
not yet built, is where the state confirms them). Type 1 is a single overall
composite score. Types 2–6 bring in more than one criterion: a composite
plus a floor, a composite plus another source, a compensatory combination,
tiered or discretionary pathways (a **pathway** is one route to exit), or a
domain profile. For those, `$policy_as_whole` would feed the whole rule's
pass/fail outcome through the same consistency and J analysis. Which
criterion drives the result comes from Prep 2's crosswalk and Check 3's
contested zone.

```{r}
spec_exit_types(spec)
spec_has_type(spec, 2:6)
```

```{r}
#| output: asis
cat(res$meta$policy_as_whole_note)
```

The simulated spec is Type 1, so the slot is `NULL` and does not apply.
**Under Types 2–6 it is also `NULL` today**: it applies but is not built,
and `res$meta$pending` lists it. Two `$j_optimal` flags already help there;
both are `FALSE` unless the spec declares a Type from 2 to 6.
`RULE_IS_TERM` is `TRUE` when the marked threshold is one term of a pathway
that also requires another criterion. `RULE_IS_ROUTE` is `TRUE` when another
pathway, or another term of an "any" pathway, lets students below it exit.
Either way the marked line is one piece of the rule, and the figure's legend
says so.

## Render the stage report

On the simulated data:

```{r}
#| eval: false
render_step("check4")
```

This writes Word and HTML to `reports/` and scans them for student
identifiers. The example report on the simulated data is
[on the project site](../check4_consistency.html).

For your state, run the stage on your bundle, save the results outside the
folder you share, and render from them:

```{r}
#| eval: false
res <- run_check4(my_bundle, my_spec)
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(res, "results/check4_results.rds")

files <- render_step("check4",
                     spec_file = normalizePath("specs/XX_EL_Spec.R"),
                     results_file = "results/check4_results.rds",
                     check_disclosure = FALSE)
check_output_disclosure(files, my_bundle)
```

Without `results_file`, the document runs on the simulated data whatever
spec you pass. Give `spec_file` as a full path, as above: the document
renders in a temporary folder, where a relative path does not resolve. Call
`render_step()` from a folder with no `R/` subfolder; otherwise the document
tries to load that folder as the package source and fails. The built-in scan
knows only the simulated bundle, so turn it off and run
`check_output_disclosure()` against your own students' identifiers instead.
